explanations.answer: Thanksgiving songs with cymbals and harps
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the verse says it plainly: the Levites came "…to celebrate the joyous dedication with thanksgiving and singing, accompanied by cymbals, harps, and lyres." Cymbals, harps AND lyres, baker. That's a whole lineup for one celebration.

explanations.answer: Victory shouts with drums and flutes
explanations.explanation: Close on the energy, but not on the details. The verse says the celebration was with "…thanksgiving and singing…" The instruments it names are cymbals, harps and lyres, and drums and flutes aren't on that list.

explanations.answer: Dancing songs with tambourines and pipes
explanations.explanation: I love the party spirit, I really do. But the verse names "…thanksgiving and singing…" with cymbals, harps and lyres. Tambourines and pipes didn't make the guest list for this verse.

Right on the money. Verse 30 says, "After the priests and Levites had purified themselves, they purified the people, the gates, and the wall." They started with themselves, then moved on to everything else. That's like me wiping off my mustache before I touch the dough.

Anoint is a real word for setting things apart, but it's not the word in this verse. Verse 30 says the priests and Levites "purified" themselves, then the people, the gates and the wall. Same crowd and same list, just a different word.
Clothing the gates and the wall would be quite a sight. I'd be out there fitting the Dung Gate for an apron. But verse 30 says they purified themselves, the people, the gates and the wall.

explanations.answer: Along the top of the wall
explanations.explanation: That's it. Nehemiah says, "…I brought the leaders of Judah up on the wall…" and the first choir was to "…proceed along the top of the wall to the right…" Up high, right on top of the wall. I'd have wanted that view myself.

Good guess, since marching down the street is how most parades go. But verse 31 puts them up on the wall. Nehemiah brought the leaders up there himself, and the first choir went along the top of the wall.

explanations.answer: Around the outside of the city
explanations.explanation: That's a long walk, but it's not what the verse says. Nehemiah says he brought the leaders "…up on the wall…" and the first choir proceeded "…along the top of the wall…" They stayed on top of it, and it was the dedication of the wall itself.

Yes, the Dung Gate. Verse 31 says the first choir was to proceed along the top of the wall "…to the right, toward the Dung Gate." Nehemiah appointed that choir to go that direction, so that's the gate to remember.
The Valley Gate is a real gate in Jerusalem. Nehemiah went out through it at night to look over the broken walls (Nehemiah 2:13). But in this verse the first choir heads toward the Dung Gate.

The Horse Gate is a real gate too, and it was among the gates repaired earlier in the book (Nehemiah 3:28). It's just not the one in this verse. Verse 31 says the first choir proceeded "…toward the Dung Gate."

That's the one. Verse 36 says the instruments were "…prescribed by David the man of God." The text gives David that title right there. Zechariah and his associates were playing with the instruments David prescribed.

Good thinking, because Moses, Israel's leader, is also called "…the man of God." in Scripture (Deuteronomy 33:1). But in this verse, the instruments are "…prescribed by David the man of God." Same title, different man.
Elijah isn't in this verse, baker. Here the instruments were "…prescribed by David the man of God." The text gives that title to David.

Nehemiah is in this scene, but he's not up front with the first choir. Verse 36 ends with this line: "Ezra the scribe led the procession." Nehemiah says he followed the second choir along the wall (Nehemiah 12:38). So the first choir's procession belongs to Ezra.
That's right. Verse 36 says, "Ezra the scribe led the procession." So Ezra was up front with the first choir. Nehemiah was off following the second choir (Nehemiah 12:38).

You've got it. Nehemiah says, "…I followed it with half the people along the top of the wall…" The first group had half the leaders, and this one had half the people. Imagine the noise of all that marching on a wall.

Horsemen are a fun picture, but they aren't in this passage. Verse 38 says Nehemiah followed the second choir "…with half the people…" Besides, I think a bunch of horses on top of a wall would make everybody nervous.

Gatekeepers do show up later in this passage, serving with the singers (Nehemiah 12:45). But for this walk, verse 38 says Nehemiah followed the second choir "…with half the people…" That's who the text names.

Yes, the house of God. Verse 40 says, "The two thanksgiving choirs then stood in the house of God…" They headed off in opposite directions and ended up in the same place, like two bakers who take different routes and meet at the same cooling rack.
A tent is a fair guess, but it's not the word here. Verse 40 says, "The two thanksgiving choirs then stood in the house of God…" That's where they ended up.

A garden would be a pretty spot, and I'd happily haul a cookie box out there. But verse 40 says the choirs "…stood in the house of God…" Not a garden, baker. After all that walking on the wall, God's house is where they landed.

explanations.answer: God had given them great joy
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, word for word. Verse 43 says they offered great sacrifices, "…rejoicing because God had given them great joy." The joy came from God, so that's where the credit goes.
Enemies leaving would be something to cheer about, I'll give you that. But verse 43 doesn't mention enemies. It says they were "…rejoicing because God had given them great joy."

explanations.answer: The king had canceled their taxes
explanations.explanation: Oh, a canceled bill would get me cheering too! But taxes never come up in this verse. The text says they were "…rejoicing because God had given them great joy."
Hold on, baker. Verse 43 says, "The women and children also rejoiced…" So the men weren't the only ones rejoicing. The women and children were in on it too.
That's right. Verse 43 says, "The women and children also rejoiced…" It wasn't a men-only party. The text says it was "…so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar."
Yes! Verse 43 says the joy of Jerusalem "…was heard from afar." It didn't stay in one spot. People far from the city could hear it.
The choirs did stand in the house of God, but the sound didn't stay there. Verse 43 says "…the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar." That's a long way from inside the temple.

explanations.answer: It stopped at the city gates
explanations.explanation: You'd think the new wall and gates would hold the noise in. But verse 43 says "…the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar." Those gates did not stop it.

explanations.answer: They rejoiced over the priests and Levites serving
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. Verse 44 says the portions were gathered "…because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving." The people were glad about the service, and that's why they brought in their share.

explanations.answer: A prophet had warned them to do it
explanations.explanation: Hold the prophet, friend! Verse 44 never mentions one. It gives the reason itself: "…because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving." The giving came out of their gladness.

explanations.answer: They were afraid a famine was coming
explanations.explanation: Fear of a famine would be a reason to stock up, but the verse doesn't say that. Verse 44 says the portions were gathered "…because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving." It was gladness, not worry.
Right. Verse 45 says the service was done "…as David and his son Solomon had prescribed." A father and son both had a hand in how this service was set up. Solomon is the son the verse names.
Absalom was one of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:3), so it's a fair guess. But verse 45 names "…David and his son Solomon…" Solomon is the son in this one.
Adonijah was another of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:4), so you're in the right family. But verse 45 says the service was done "…as David and his son Solomon had prescribed." Solomon is the name here.

True. Verse 47 says, "…in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel contributed the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers." All Israel pitched in. Everybody had a hand in supporting the ones who served.

This one is true, though it's easy to doubt. Verse 47 says, "…in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel contributed the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers." It says all Israel, not just a few.
That's it. Verse 47 says the Levites "…set aside daily portions for the descendants of Aaron." Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). The portions passed along from one group to the next.
Moses was Israel's leader, and he was Aaron's brother (Exodus 4:14), so you're close. But verse 47 says the Levites set aside portions "…for the descendants of Aaron." Aaron is the name in the verse.
Korah was a Levite (Numbers 16:1), so he's in the right tribe. But verse 47 says the Levites "…set aside daily portions for the descendants of Aaron." Aaron is the name this verse uses.
